So that, if it were agreeable to all parties concerned we could much more easily describe the boundary by saying that w'e w'ould follow the railway line to the third meridian, thence northerly bv the third meridian to the north line of township 44, thence w'est along the northern line of township 44 to the Calgary and Edmonton railw'ay line, and then follow the Calgary and Edmonton line until it strikes the west line of range 26. That w'ould practically carry the line down to the boundary. That would be a more convenient description of the boundary than the one I have here, but I adopted this for the purpose of getting a well defined natural boundary. However, if the third meridian is considered suitable from the point of view of my hon. friend, whose constituency it is in, it would be much more easily described and would seem to be quite as satisfactory as the present boundary.

Did I understand the minister to say that the terms under which an old settler, who had already obtained the patent for his homestead, would be allowed to acquire a pre-emption were as set out in the Bill of last year? I am just looking up the old Bill, and as far as I can see the terms apply to both parties in just the same way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What are the terms to the old settler iu the old Bill ?
There is just one set of terms as far as I can see, and they are the same terms as are given to the new settler under the new Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Five years ?
Five years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I merely stated to the committee what I supposed was the way In which the error had arisen, but, certainly, it was an error and there was no reason for it. Our intention has been to make the two cases conform as closely as cirsumstances permitted.

Of course the minister has not yet replied to the point which was made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that even now the new settler is going to get very much better terms in connection with his pre-emption than the old settler; that is to say, there is no obligation upon the new settler who takes up a preemption to do any work whatever on that pre-emption. He can do all his work on the homestead and he is permitted to purchase a pre-emption without doing any work upon it. It would be very much better policy, as I have already suggested, to extend the same right to the older settlers on the condition of extensive cultivation in lieu of residence on the land. I believe it would be very much better for the land and you will not meet with the trouble which was suggested by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Gfreenway) last year of making men pick up their goods, leave their present holdings and start out for new districts, depopulating the old districts in order to populate the new. I think it would be better not to force a man to go into residence on a pre-emption.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In so far as a reply to the statement made by the hon. member for North Toronto is concerned, I do not think there is any reply to be made. The hon. gentleman stated the facts of the case as set out in the Bill and there is nothing to be said about it. With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for Qu'-Appelle that it would be sound public policy to permit the acquisition of purchased land in this area without settlement, while that would be certainly a very popular policy in the part of the country which is already settled, it would be an equally unpopular policy in the part of the country which is to be settled and, although it would be a way of securing popularity with a number of people, it would not be sound public policy with regard to the settlement of the country and, for my part, I do not feel I could endorse it.

I cannot see why it should be unpopular in the new districts. A man could not comply with the cultivation conditions which he would be called upon to do in this case without sending some one up to do the work for him. There are many new comers in the country who are unable to go out and take up homesteads for themselves. This is a way in which a man could be sent to a new district to do the work on the homestead and later become a settler himself in that particular district. It is the difference between leaving the hired man at home or sending him out to the new district, instead of going yourself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The most important feature of the land settlement policy is the bodily presence of the man who is interested in the land upon the land. The hon. gentleman himself has been the most vigorous of any member of the House in attacking the government because of alleged, deviation from this policy, absolutely insisting upon its being carried out. That is our policy. We may have failed in this or that particular instance, but it is our policy, we do carry it out and we cannot see that we would be warranted in absolutely departing from it and allowing non-resident ownership in a vast area of 28.000,000 acres. It would be such a radical departure from that which has been considered to be the policy of the government of our predecessors as well as ourselves, as the policy which has been at the very foundation of the true settlement of the west ever since it began, that I would not like to endorse such a very radical departure.

Did you always have resident ownership? We so frequently get applications from men in the west who declare that men own homesteads who have not been on them at all. I have a letter from a man near Lloydminster who says that a hotel keeper there who is engaged in the hotel business has a lot on which he has never been at all, but people cannot have the homestead cancelled. The man says there are many others in the same position. You can never get them cancelled.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the facts are as my hon. friend states the government's administration is not in line with its policy. I have no excuse to offer for that condition of affairs, except that it has not come to my personal attention. If it exists it is not because of our policy but contrary to it. I

wish to move the following amendment to subsection 5 of section 28 :
The price payable for land under this section shall be $3 per acre, and such price shall be payable one-third at the time entry is made and the balance in five equal annual instalments, and interest shall be payable at the rate of five per cent per annum at the end of each year from date of the said entry on the amount remaining unpaid at the time; provided that on completion of the requirements under this section for obtaining letters patent for such purchased homestead, payment in full may be made for the same and letters patent therefor may thereupon issue.
That conforms to the section in the corresponding clause,

The minister will have to have non-resident ownership any way for any old settler who takes advantage of this clause will have to leave his old homestead. I presume if there is a considerable amount of improvements and cultivationi insisted1 on there would have to be residence by some one.
In subsection 10, I see the words ' who fails to secure a patent for his free homestead.' I think that really means who fails to perform the duties necessary to secure the patent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is for that reason that we put in the saving clause, ' at the minister's discretion.' My hon. friend knows that it is absolutely necessary in the administration of our homestead law to prevent, so far as we can possibly do so, trafficking in homesteads. Therefore we make the declaration as definite and sweeping as we can. Yet there may be cases in which the act may be done innocently, and there should 1/e some discretion to save the right of property in such cases.

It might be done innocently, or it might be done legally with the consent of the government. After a man had made certain improvements on a piece of land, a new man might come along and purchase his improvements.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That would be entirely illegal ; we do not recognize that at all.' If we did, we might just as well admit the practice of selling homesteads. We have to set our faces absolutely against anything of that kind. But of course there are cases that are deserving of consideration, and we want to have authority to give them that consideration.
Mr. M, S. McCarthy. Would the section as it is worded cover an agreement for a lease ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. The idea is that he will get the entry when he has completed his duties on his first homestead. Either we have to deprive him of the privilege of entry prior to the issue of the patent or we must make the holding of the entry subject to the issue of the patent if we are to make the provision effective according to the spirit and intent of the Act.
On section 31-assignments of homesteads.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would not think so.

McCarthy. A might get B to make a homestead entry on a certain quarter-section, put up a certain amount of money and allow him to go on and do the work necessary to comply with the regulations, and make an agreement with him to lease it for ninety-nine years, which would practically be a title. Would the minister's intention to absolutely prohibit traffic in homesteads forbid a case of that kind ?
Under what circumstances would the minister declare that a patent shall not issue?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This provision is merely a saving provision. Assuming that there may be such circumstances as my hon. friend suggests, though it is not probable that there are, the act may have been done ignorantly of the provision, and therefore we think it is very desirable that the minister should have this discretion.
Has the minister had any such cases since he has been in office ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Such a case may have been dealt with departmentally without having reached me, but I have no knowledge of any such case.
A man might in many ways give to another man a consideration to abandon his entry which might be perfeetly legal.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This section would not. I think that the person who homesteaded could never acquire title to his homestead under that agreement.
McCarthy. I think he could, from the affidavit he would be required to make when he proved up on his homestead, unless it has been amended in recent years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, that would be contrary to our intention.
There must be cases in which it is quite obvious that there has been some consideration paid for abandonment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Such cases may occur and do occur, but our purpose is to prevent their occurrence so far as we can. I am under the impression that the class of eases mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary would be properly provided for rather in the affidavit of entry and of proof of compliance with the conditions than in this

clause regarding abandonment. The suggestion of my hon. friend is something new, but certainly there are possibilities in it which would have to be met in some way.
On section 8-sale of agricultural lands.

I would like to suggest that all these orders in council should be published at once in the ' Gazette ' so that the general public may know what is being done. I have hunted for a good many of these orders in council in the ' Gazette,' and have not been able to And them. I imagine that a good many of them have not been published for some time after they were passed and some not at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am under the impression that all sales of land authorized by orders in council are published in the ' Gazette.' If they are not, I think it would be very proper that they should be.
May others than homesteaders purchase these fractional quarter-sections ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under our printed regulations we sell to the owner of the adjoining land whether he is a "homesteader or not.
McCarthy. Would it be possible for the minister to specify in the Act the grounds authorizing the sale of lands? The section leaves him rather a wide discretion.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course it is pretty hard to make a provision without giving some discretion. In practice, we sell a fraction to the owner of the adjoining land, but there might possibly be an owner who would not be inclined to acquire the land and some other person might want it, and there is no reason why the land should be tied up. Our regulations provide that we must sell to the owner of the adjoining land, but these regulations may be varied from time to time and the Act cannot. So that if we put such a provision in the Act, we might tie up a piece of land without due regard to the public interests.	.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: All these orders in council relating to the disposal of any part of the public domain should be brought down and laid on the table of parliament in the first fifteen days of every session.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That might answer the same purpose as publishing in the ' Gazette.' I have no objection to publishing in the ' Gazette ' but that would be fairly cum-berous and perhaps not necessary.

Laying on the table is no doubt very necessary, but that does not come to the knowledge of many people. I think it would be a safeguard if such sales and regulations were published in the Canada ' Gazette.' The public would then know what is going on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister might add a clause at the end of the Bill to that effect.
Mr. OLIVER, As we go through the Bill, we may arrive at a conclusion that will meet all views and embody that in one section.
On section 33,
Land suitable for grazing but not adapted for agriculture, or hay or marsh lands, may be sold or leased under regulations made by the Governor in Council.

These regulations ought to be published. How is the minister to differentiate between these three classes of land? For instance, hay or marsh lands during one period may become agricultural lands at a later period.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is for that reason we have left the provision subject to regulation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As a matter of fact what is the practice of the department in respect of determining the character of land. On whose report does the minister decide ? Suppose I should apply for a certain area as grazing land, how would the minister deal with it ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That would be dealt with under the regulations regarding grazing. The application must be made in a certain form and state certain facts as to the lands and the ownership of stock, and there being no other rights interfered with. We have an oflieial whose time is entirely devoted to that work. He inspects and reports upon the nature of the land and as to whether there is any one in occupation, and whether there are cattle owned by others than the applicants which are ranging on it or in this vicinity. He reports to us and then we decide whether to issue the lease or not.
On section 34,
Lands unsuitable for cultivation without the aid of irrigation, or lands required in connection with any system of irrigation, may be sold or leased in such manner and under such terms and conditions as are fixed by the Governor in Council, and subject to the provisions of the Irrigation Act.

How are you to determine what lands are unsuitable for cultivation without the aid of irrigation ? Irrigation ditches have been dug in the Northwest and then abandoned, because it was found subsequently the lands were suitable for cultivation without irrigation.
Mi-. OLIVER. That is a matter upon which it is difficult to arrive at a fixed conclusion, as conditions change. There may be a series of years, in every one of which a certain tract of country would require irrigation, and then for a succeeding series of years, there would be no need of it. We

have to be guided by the general belief as to the sufficiency or insufficiency of rainfall in the country affected, during sufficient periods to warrant the expenditure on irrigation. Generally speaking, southern Alberta and, western Saskatchewan, east of the foothills and west of the Coteau Missouri may be bettered in some years by irrigation. If any one desires to make an expenditure that will irrigate any particular tract of land, we would feel warranted in giving him the privilege.
MCCARTHY. Suppose certain sections of the country would be made fit by drainage ?	-
Whereabouts ?
McCarthy'. I understand that the local administration of the province of Alberta is undertaking drainage works.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Each individual drainage area is comparatively small and therefore the expenditure also small. The drainage would therefore be a provincial rather than a Dominion work. But in the ease of irrigation, the area is large, and the possibility of irrigation depends upon the flow of the streams which flow from one province into another. Therefore, irrigation does not lend itself to provincial control as drainage does.
On section 35-water-power.
McCarthy. This section was not in the Bill as introduced last year. Would the minister give us some reason why it is inserted in this Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There was a section in the Bill last yeax-, but it was not nearly so com-jxrehensive as this. Both the sections of last year and the one of this year are practically new, that is we have no specific provision in the old Lands Act for dealing with water-power^ There was a provision for the reservation of land on which there was water-powei1, but there was no provision for dealing with the water-power itself. As the waters of the western provinces, which are under the jurisdiction of this Act, are regulated under the control of the Dominion government by the terms of the Irrigation Act, it has been the custom to deal with the development of watei'-powers under the terms of that Act, but it was found in practice, and before the practice had gone very far, that as the Irrigation Act had not been framed for the utilization of the water for power purposes, its provisions were not applicable, and it was necessary, in view of the possibility of water-power developments, and the desirability of having it developed, to make provisions under which the water-powers might be developed under conditions which would, in the first place, be fair to those who desire to make developments, and, in the second place, to the public who had the interest in the wrater and who had an in-Mr. OLIVER.
terest in the ultilization of the water. Therefore, we have placed in the Bill provisions especially for that purpose. The provision has been very carefully drafted, and we believe that on the closest inspection it will be found to be adequate for the purpose. We allow the utilization of the power subject to certain conditions and provide that the utilization may take place subject to such charge as may be made for the privilege of using the water, and that any charges for use of the development may be subject to regulation by the government.

Is the minister sui-e that provision is made that there will be no difficulty about carrying the water over the land after it is taken from the stream ? It seems to me there was some difficulty about that in our country, at Middle Fork Falls for instance. The land was purchased by some individual, and he made some exorbitant claim about giving the privilege to take water across the land. I hope that is provided for, as it may be vex*y serious to important interests and to the people at lai'ge.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is exactly the condition as it was. There was no provision that would apply to the case that my lion. tTiend has mentioned. But, if he will notice, subsection 3 of this section, makes provision for that particular instance by applying the provisions of the Railway Act-that is to say, applying the expropriation clauses of the Railway Act to the requirements of the development for water-power.
On section 37-mineral lands.

We were dealing with a clause the other evening which dealt, to some degree, with the same subject, lands containing minerals. I still think the homesteader should have first privilege of purchasing. It might not be applicable to say that he should have the whole area of his homestead. That might do In the case of iron or coal, but for gold or other precious metals, it would be cut down to a smaller area. But I see no reason why the homesteader should not have some of the first privileges of buying these mineral rights at the upset price or the price that the government offers them to other people.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is a great deal to be said for the principle my hon. friend has mentioned, and in some of our regulations dealing with these matters at the present time we provide that the settler shall have priority. For instance, in the case of petroleum the settler has the surface right. I am not sure whether the present coal regulations make the same provision, but I know in the recent regulations as to the sale of coal lands we apply that provision, and the homesteader has priority. The principle of giving priority to the homesteader is a very proper one as long as it is not

carried to an abuse. But 1 do not think it is advisable to make the provision the hon. gentleman suggests. The proper way to give the priority of which he speaks is to do it in the regulations dealing with the disposition of minerals. If it should be found, in drafting the regulations, that it is possible to preserve the priority right of. a homesteader it will be done, but I do not think it would be advisable to embody a provision to that effect in the Act.
On section 39-exchange of school lands.

McCarthy. I would like to hear from the minister the reasons why he continues in this Bill to keep control of the school lands and the school fund in the new provinces. It occurs to me that it would be better that the control of these should be handed over to the provinces. Now the lands are sold at public auction by the Dominion and the funds are invested for the benefit of the provinces ; why, therefore, should not the control of them be handed over to the provinces? There can be no reason for the federal government continuing to control the land and the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The matter that my hon. friend mentions is one that might come up for consideration. As I have said already, I do not undertake any radical change in the Bill beyond what seemed to me necessary for administration purposes, with the one exception of the pre-emption and purchased homestead clauses, the reasons of which I have already given. The setting apart of lands for higher education and placing the school lands directly under the coptrol of the provinces, are both questions of general policy rather than of departmental administration, and I have not undertaken to deal with either of them. I am merely continuing in this Act the provisions in regard to school lands which existed in the preceding Act.

Does any reason occur to the hon. gentleman why it should not be done ? Unless there is some good reason why the federal administration should continue to control the lands, it seems to me they can be better controlled by the respective provinces. There is another question. Is it the intention to continue setting aside lands in the northern part of the province for school purposes, where the surveys have not been executed at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provision covers all the townships that may be surveyed where-ever they are.

The minister might regard it as almost a certainty that where-ever there is an exchange made for school lands before the survey, the settler invariably takes the best land. I do not think the school fund is likely to get land equally as good.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have had a great deal of experience in the choice of land by the pioneers, and I have not found the facts to be as my hon. friend has stated. The pioneer does not always make the wisest choice. I have already stated the principle we have recently adopted in connection with school lands, which I'think will to some extent balance the condition my hon. friend deplores, if it exists at all to the extent he thinks, that is to say, that where we>
find a piece of land, a quarter-section, under reservation, held out from settlement for one reason or another as a pre-emption, or for timber, or for water supply, or something of that kind, when it is decided no longer to withhold this section, and when settlement has grown up around it, instead of offering it for homesteading we are now scheduling that quarter-section as school lands, so as to give the school fund the benefit in that way of land that has become especially valuable to compensate for land such as the hon. gentleman has spoken of.

The minister was speaking of the abandonment of the principle of setting apart school lands in the territory outside the organized provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. It seems to me that the setting apart of a certain amount of surveyed land for educational purposes is one of the best things which could be done for the future of that country. Although the minister says he has not made any changes in principle in this Act, yet I find in a foot note in regard to this section that it is stated that this is a change, that the original provision, was that throughout all Dominion lands which are surveyed certain sections should be set apart for school purposes. The foot note says it is now considered inexpedient to make that provision outside of the three provinces. I would like to hear the minister's reasons for taking that ground. I think that there may be portions of country outside those provinces which will be settled heavily some day, and we ought to provide for public education in them in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As a matter of theory, of course, my hon. friend is right. But in drafting the Act it did not seem to be necessary to make a provision for an instance that would not be likely to arise. In the extension of the two new provinces to the 60th parallel, and the expected extension of the province of Manitoba to the same distance north, it seemed to us that we would thereby include practically all the territory that would come under survey, that is, under the system of Dominion land surveys, for a great many years. We thought it would not be sound public policy to make any reierv th n of such limited areas as would be likely, in that far northern country, to be found suit-

able to settlement. The principle of the reservation of two sections in each township is applied under the belief that the whole township, and practically the whole country, is suitable for settlement.
Has it not been the practice of the department to set apart certain lands in the railway belt of British Columbia for certain purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
It seems to me to be a very proper provision to set apart a portion of the land in all these new countries for that purpose.
Can the minister tell me if the rate of interest has been reduced recently on the defered payments on school lands bought from the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware that it has, but I would rather think that it has not been.

I do not suggest that is has been since the minister has occupied his present position, but I think that a few years ago the rate was reduced. I would be glad if the minister would find out and let me know before the Bill goes out of committee.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. I am just informed that some years ago the general rate of interest on payments to the government was reduced to five per cent.

McCarthy. I suppose, the minister could not tell us what the reduction amounted to annually or the size of the fund at the present time. Some of these lands recently have been sold at very large figures. For instance, land sold for $55 an acre near Saskatoon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I can bring the information to the House later on, as to the present amount of the fund, when the reduction took place, if it did take place, and the amount of the fund at that time.
On section 39, paragraph 2-exchange of sehool lands.
Do I understand this section to give the minister power to take Indian reserves for irrigation purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

In line 4 page 27, referring to the sale of a school site it provides that in no case is the amount of land ' to exceed an area of two acres.' Does that mean that you can only take two acres as a site for a school house?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
That is not always suitable. Sometimes two acres of Dominion lands may be more suitable for the purpose than two acres of school lands. The school lands are not always situated at the proper place.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is taking the argument from the wrong end. Without any legislation we could dispose of any ordinary government lands to the board of school trustees for a school site, but we cannot do that with school lands, and this is to provide that we may do it with school lands.

Does the minister think two acres sufficient for a school site? Perhaps it is generally, but there may be circumstances under which a difficulty would arise, because, in addition to the school, you require to have a stable and a well.
It should be made five acres in that country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not particular as to the amount. Of course, we are administering school lauds as trustees, and we do not wish to make a break upon a quarter-section that would seriously reduce its ordinary value. Two acres oat of 160 will really not reduce its value more than the price of the two acres, but it is easy to suppose that you might increase the area that might be taken out of a quarter-section and thereby seriously depreciate the value of the balance of the quarter-section. I am satisfied that even five acres would be no serious injury to the quarter-section but I desired to place that view before hon. gentleman, and if they still think that five acres might be taken without seriously depleting the value of the balance I am willing to make it five acres.
At any rate it should be three acres taking into consideration that you must always have stables and wells'.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Suppose we compromise on four?
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That the word ' two ' where it occurs in the fourth line from the top of page 27 be changed to ' four.'

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems to me that there are a great many unnecessary words in this section, and that it would have been better if 30 per cent of these words had been left out. There are so many words in it that it is almost impossible to understand it. For example, you have five lines in one place that you could leave out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not going to dispute my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I will point out some instances to the minister. Look at line 24, page 2G. If you leave out after the word 1 but ' down to the word ' until,' five lines below, you will have exactly the same sense if you insert the word * not,' so that it would read :

But not until other Dominion lands of equal value as nearly as may be have been' selected in lieu thereof.
It would mean exactly the same ; you simply avoid five lines of vain repetition. Then, on page 27 you deal with price at two different places, making the sentence extremely awkward. It should have been drafted more in this way :
The minister may, forthwith, sell to the board of school trustees for the district for which the same is required, such portion of school lands in no case exceeding an area of four acres at a price of not less than $10 an acre-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Which must front on a road allowance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You leave that in.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then it would not read as my hon. friend has said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps not just in that connection, but there is no need of dealing with the price in two different places.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have every confidence In my hon. friend's views as to the drafting of the section but the first part, that is the part before the proviso has passed through the hands of the Justice Department. The proviso, I think, is the work of the law clerk of the Interior Department. I would not like to amend the drafting off-hand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would not suggest that. In a great many statutes introduced this session there is a very great redundancy. The minister can see for himself that if the last half of subsection 2 were reduced in the way I have spoken of, it would mean exactly the same thing and be better expressed.
On section 40-terms of payments for school lands.
What is done with the interest on the unpaid principal? Is that payable to the province, or does that go into capital account?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: All funds, both principal and interest, accruing from the sale of school lands are the property of the province and form part of the trust fund for the jn'ovince.
It seems to me the interest on the unpaid balance might fairly go to the province at once.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That possibly would be right, but I think it might better be debated as a question of financing and of the relations between the provinces and the Dominion than on the provisions of this Bill, which proposes no alteration in the condition.

Clause 42 provides for the interest being paid annually into the province.
On section 42-payment of interest on trust fund.
That does not cover the point raised by the hon. member for Qu-'Appelle.

I cannot help think, as the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. M. S. McCarthy) suggested, that it would be advisable that these trust funds for each of the provinces should be in the hands of the provincial authorities. I think it would be a very good step to take, and if I remember rightly, our friends on the other side of the House, who came from Manitoba, believed very strongly in that principle in the days gone by.

I was pointing out that this section does not cover the point raised as to the payment to the province of the 5 per cent on the unpaid balances. That would mean that the 5 per cent interest on deferred payments goes into the capital account, and that the interest on that 5 per cent is paid over to the province.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is correct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does not the minister think that the interest ought to go to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that the question of the disposition of the money realized from the sale of school lands is a matter rather of finance and adjustment between the provinces and the Dominion than pertaining directly to the administration of Dominion lands. These sections only appear here as an incident. They have to be embodied somewhere, and they are embodied in this Bill; but as this Bill does not make any change in the conditions regarding them, and as the questions raised by my hon. friends are of the character I have mentioned, I would think that the discus* sion of these points might be taken up with profit on another occasion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But if the Bill passes in its present form, they cannot be taken up with effect on another occasiou, because the law would be fixed. Take a concrete instance. You sell $10,000 worth of school lands for cash. That sum of $10,000 is at once invested in securities and the interest goes annually to the province for all time to come. You sell the same quantity of school lands, and the payments are deferred-$1,000 a year for ten consecutive years. In that case the interest is paid to the Dominion government. It does not go to the province, but only the interest on the annual interest goes to the province. So that the mere accident of deferring the payments changes altogether the financial situation as between the province and the Dominion. What is suggested on this side of the House is that such an accident should not lessen tlie annual financial benefit which

any province receives from the sale of school lands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I quite appreciate the argument; but, while of course it is quite corn-patent to discuss the matter in dealing with this Bill, it is a matter of general policy involving transactions between the Dominion and the province that I think might very well be taken up as a question by itself.
But you would have to alter this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly, when the time came. But for the present and for the purposes of this Bill we are simply carrying forward the provision that already exists. We are not presenting a new phase of the question. We are simply asking that the present arrangement be continued for the time being until the matter, which has a certain gravity as a first-class question, can be dealt with in the way it deserves.

It seems to me that it is treating these provinces with a good deal of disrespect for the Dominion government to take charge of these school lands and sell them, and not even trust the provinces with the money to invest for school purposes, but invest it in securities and dole out the proceeds to the provinces. That is treating these provinces as wards o ' the nation, as if they were not able to take care of themselves. This money is intended for school purposes in the provinces, and the Dominion government simply act as trustees. These provinces ought to be fit to be trusted with the management of their own business; they ought to be out of tutelage and wardship. If they had the handling of the money, they could probably invest It in securities that would yield greater interest than the Dominion government can obtain, and be equally good with, the securities in which the Dominion government invests it. It seems to me to be the duty of the Dominion government to hand over to the provinces these school lands, to be disposed of in whatever way would be most advantageous to them; and I should think that they, being on the ground, and having a better and fuller knowledge of the circumstances surrounding these lands than this government can have, could better administer them than the federal government. You have granted a certain measure of selfgovernment to these provinces. I think they ought to be granted a complete measure of self-government and be allowed to administer these school lands for themselves.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I agree entirely with that view. The Dominion government is simply acting as a trustee for the provinces in respect to the management t>f the school lands and the investment of the proceeds from their sale. You may have trustees for minor and other persons incapable Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
of taking care of their own affairs; but you do not usually have a trustee for a person who is perfectly capable of managing his own affairs. While we have been talking of the minor question of interest, there seems to be no reason why we should continue to manage these lands and hand over to the provinces the interest annually. The provinces might be relied on to administer these lands to the best advantage for their own purposes.

I agree strongly with the point that has been taken with regard to the capital account, but still more strongly with the point with regard to the annual interest. This government decides that it will sell the lands in ten annual instalments. The hon. leader of the opposition has pointed out how that works. $10,000 worth of lands were sold, $1,000 received by the government the first year and then paid into the fund, and the province received 3 per cent or $30 a year. The Dominion government, on the other hand, received 5 per cent on the remaining $9,000 or $450 a year. And all they pay to the province for school purposes is $30 the first year. Of course the amount increases slightly the second year and continues to increase as each year's interest is paid in. It seems to me the province should have the benefit of all the interest.

I would like to know the views of the Minister of the Interior regarding the question I raised as to the transfer of the school lands to the various provinces for which these lands are now held in trust. Does he think that the provinces should remain in that sense the wards of the nation, or does he think they are now fit for selfgovernment ? Does he think they are quite as able to handle these lands and invest the proceeds for school purposes as the federal government ? Does he not think they are better qualified because they are closer to the lands themselves ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The business of the Minister of the Interior is to administer the lands of the west according to the policy of the government. The policy of the government with regard to the school lands is laid down in the Act. The Minister of the Interior is charged with the responsibility of providing the government with a policy regarding the administration of the lands for settlement purposes and generally for the development of the west, but he is not charged with the responsibility of laying down a policy with regard to dealing with the school lands. That is a matter pertaining to the general policy of the government in its relation with (the several provinces. I would not feel warranted in undertaking to state what is the policy of the government as regards the school lands except as it is expressed in the statute. With regard to other branches of the land question. I am quite

ready to state my views ; but as regards tUe school lands, that is a matter for consideration and discussion as one of government policy and not departmental policy.

The minister is drawing a fine distinction between the various classes of lands, that It is Impossible for me to see it. So far as the provinces are concerned, the administration of the school lands is quite as* important as the administration of any other lands. The educational idea is as important as any other-in fact, more important perhaps than many others. "Therefore, if it is necessary for the Minister of the Interior to find a policy for the government with regard to other lands it is just as necessary for him to define a policy with regard to the school lands and try to get the government to adopt it. I cannot see the distinction which he draws between the two classes of lands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The difference is this, that in the case of the administration of agricultural, mineral, timber and grazing lands, we are dealing with the rights of individuals. That is naturally necessarily a departmental matter; but the general question of the adjustment of school lands accounts between the Dominion government and the provincial government is necessarily not a departmental matter but a matter of government policy, which pertains rather to the Department of Finance and the Department of the Secretary of State than to the Department of the Interior.

The government provides a policy under which the Minister of the Interior administers fthe other lands. The government provides a policy and crystallizes that policy into the form of law, and it is under that law the minister administers these lands which go to private individuals ; and it is equally by force of a law formulated by the government itself that the minister administers these school lands. He sells them when the circumstances call for a sale; lie administers them just the same as he does the other lands, so that I still fail to see the distinction which the hon. minister draws. I think if we had the minister's real view as to what should be done with the lands, it would not be "very far from what I have expressed.

There is nothing about the policy of the government with regard to school lands, which is unusual. Our local legislature of Manitoba for twenty years passed resolutions asking that the school lands be handed over to them ; but during the administration of Sir John Macdonald in 1872-3-4, and right along, under succeeding Conservative administrations, to 1890, this same policy was pursued. I was in the local legislation from 1882 up to 1900, and there was hardly a session when we did
not pass resolutions, asking the Dominion government to hand over the school lands to the province. The policy of the previous government has been continued by the present. I am in favour of those lands being handed over to the local governments. I do not see that the federal government are making anything by keeping the administration of those lands in their own possession. They have all the trouble of administering them. One of the arguments against handing them over to the Manitoba government was that that government would have to establish a land department which would entail considerable expense and that the lands could be cheaper administered from Ottawa. I have never held that view, but would like to see the lands handed over to the provinces. I hold the view taken by the leader of the opposition that they would be as carefully administered by the different provinces as they are by this government.

My hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Jackson) has just pointed to another instance which illustrates the fact that this government has been unable to form any policy itself, but is only able to follow the policy of its predecessors. Unfortunately the hon. gentleman, although he comes from the west, and must know thoroughly the western conditions, and although he has been a member of the local legislature of Manitoba for years, has not sufficient influence on the government to induce it to change its policy and adopt a better one.

There is another reason which has just occurred to me, after listening to the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Jackson), which makes me think that the administration of the school lands by the provinces in the North-west, would be more in the interests of the school fund than their administration by the Dominion.
The Department of the Interior, as this Bill shows, has not merely to administer the school lands, but also the other lands for purposes of irrigation or other matters of that kind, which sometimes include school lands. Then the Minister of the Interior is to be himself the judge between the interests of the department in its administration for purposes of settlement and so on, and the department as trustees for the school funds. I think it would be much in the interest of the school fund, if negotiations in regard to the exchange of school lands for other lands of equal value, as set forth in the Act, were between two different parties, the authorities of the province on the one hand and the authorities of the Dominion on the other hand. And, after all, the people of the province, are very much more vitally interested in obtaining large endowments for educational purposes than the people of the Dominion generally are.

On section 44-Hudsons Bay Company lands.
Has there ever been any dispute over the area of land the Hudson's Bay Company have the right to select from?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not to my knowledge.
Have they made all selections ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Their selections are automatic. When surveys are made, their lands are fixed. We do not pass the title to them; they hold the original title.

Under this section the company is give certain rights of choice in townships on the northern bank of the North Saskatchewan. Does that apply to the tributaries of the North Saskatchewan or only to a certain area north of the main stream of the North Saskatchewan ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The wording is here, it says the North Saskatchewan river. That means the main stream.
On section 48-revenue from timber limits in unsurveyed lands.
I think that section requires a little explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The provision is the same as it has been in the present law, except that the words ' the fertile belt ' are not used in the description. A provision that the Hudson Bay Company shall receive one-twentieth of the land is dependent upon a survey, that is, their ability to exercise their rights depends upon a survey being made. However, whether there is a survey or not, in the case of a timber limit which is not in surveyed territory, although there has not been a township survey which will define the land over which they have an absolute and previous right, they are entitled to claim the twentieth of the proceeds of the limit.
In the case of a forest reserve, do you allow them still to retain their eight and twenty-six, or do you buy them out?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the Forest Reserves Act there is a provision for the exchange of lands. That provision is for the purpose of enabling us to adjust matters with the company so as to relieve the reserve from their ownership of the eight and twenty-six.
Have you done that in any case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have not concluded negotiations. I had some negotiations with the commissioner of the company two or three months ago, when he was going to England, and he intended to bring the matter before the board of directors. I hope that within the year we will have a satisfactory arrangement that will clear the Mr. LAKE.
Hudson bay lands out of these reserves. Until that is done our purpose in the reservation cannot be carried out effectually.
On section 50-title to land to pass to Hudson Bay Company.
Why do you use the expression ' three-quarter parts of sections ' ?	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In section 44, in some sections they are entitled to the whole of the eight and twenty-six ; in others, they are entitled to only three-fourths of the twenty-six.
On section 51-regulations for disposal of timber.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What does the minister understand by the expression * public competition ' ? Does it include calls for tender as well as for public auction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is the policy of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The regulations under which we are now administering timber lands provided for sale by auction only. Up to that time the sale was by tender.
Where would the auction sales be held?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: At the land agency of the district within which the timber is situated. That applies to the railway belt.
Does the government provide for having an estimate made by one of their own officers of the value of timber before offering it for sale?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a provision of the regulations. Owing to the lull in the lumber business we have not had the same demand for limits that existed a year ago. But when we have reason to believe that it would be in the public interest to offer for sale timber in any part of the country, we first have the locality viewed by an employee of the department, who informs us as to the area covered by timber, the kind of timber, and the probable boundaries that would include the valuable timber. On his report we decide whether it is such a case as would warrant us in putting it up for sale. If we decide that the timber is of such a character, or is so situated, as to warrant us in putting it up for sale, we have the berth surveyed, then we advertise it for sale by auction at the land office of the district in which the limit is situated.
How do you arrange about the cost of survey? Do you put an upset price which includes the cost of survey?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That would be our idea. In any case, the survey has to be paid for. Under the former system the person who

acquired tlie limit paid the cost of the survey, which was an expense to him over and above the bonus he paid. At present we pay the cost of the survey, and, of course, the limit is worth just that much more to the man who buys it. While we do not propose to charge it up as a matter of book-keeping, as it will work out the limit holder will pay the cost of survey, but he will pay it in the bonus he pays for the limit. The difference between the system that we worked under before and the system we work under now, is that formerly any person who wanted to have a timber berth put up, on his application it was put up. We have dropped that system now, and practically all timber is under reservation unless and until the government, in pursuance of its policy and according to the information it has, thinks it sound policy to offer it for sale.

I think that is a very wise change. But the department has, I understand, adopted a regulation that I do not think is as wise as the regulation the minister has just referred to, that is, the enforcement of the clause in the license which requires the erection of a mill cutting a certain amount. If the minister persists in that regulation, I do not think he will find that it will work out to the advantage of the general public, it certainly will not work out to the advantage of the milling industry, because, as the minister knows, there is now more lumber manufactured than there is sale for. In the interest of the lumbermen, who, after all, have some rights that ought to be considered, I do not think it would be well for the minister to persist in that regulation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman hardly expresses the case correctly. It is not a regulation.
It is part of the lease but it is not necessarily enforced. I gather that the department propose to enforce it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, the enforcement will be a matter of policy. We are not insisting upon the letter of the lease. We are not insisting upon the erection of a mill and we are not enforcing the terms of the lease except with regard to limits which have been held without operation for five years. All we are asking is that when a limit has been held without operation for five years some work be performed upon it. We issue an order to erect a mill but we say to the limit holder : If you do not want to erect a mill, if you cut so much lumber from the limit, that will be accepted in lieu of the fulfilment of the terms which require the erection of a mill. We even go further than than and say that if a certain individual, or company, owns several limits we will accept the cutting upon one of these limits of the total amount of lumber that our order requires from the whole of the limits 364
owned by the single individual or company. I think we are going a very considerable distance in accommodating our instructions to the circumstances of the case. I am quite aware that the position in regard to lumbering has changed radically within a year, and I am not going to say that it would not be fair to take that into consideration in dealing with the matter, but, for the present, I just wanted to say, in the first place, that this was not a regulation, but that we are merely acting strictly under the terms of the license.
I spoke of it as being a clause in the lease.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. We are not enforcing it up to the limit, we are giving an alternative from the terms of the license which we think is easier, and we are permitting the operation of one limit by a company owning several in enforcing this regulation.

It is not possible to cut the lumber except to cut it and pile it up in the-woods and leave it there to rot on account of the distance necessary to haul it to the mill, supposing a man has a limit upon which he has no mill. There might be a mill within ten or twelve miles, but distance would prohibit him from manufacturing except he erected a mill. Then he would be compelled to erect a mill and that would mean the throwing of an additional amount of lumber upon the market which is not able to take care of the lumber which is now upon it under natural conditions. If the policy of the government is to conserve the timber and only to have it manufactured as rapidly as the circumstances of the country required, it would seem to me that if you insisted upon the letter of the license you would be acting in contradiction to that policy. You would be insisting upon the manufacture of more lumber than the country is prepared to take care of, and, under these circumstances, and in view of the fact, as the minister has stated, that the lumber conditions in the west have radically changed within the year, it would seem to me that the strict enforcement of the regulations might be put off for another year at least until the circumstances had changed and there was a greater demand for lumber in the west.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is certainly a great deal to be said on account of the changed conditions of the lumber industry. At the time we issued this order the conditions were quite different from what they are to-day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: At what date was the order issued ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Some time last fall.
It was some time in December.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, about the same time as we changed the regulations.
You gave a year's notice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. We have no desire to embarrass the lumber industry. But, of of course we had to consider that there is that section in the lease and the conditions being as they were two years ago, or even a year and a half ago, we felt that with that provision in the lease we would be expected to do something towards its enforcement. We could not very well ignore the fact that it was there and that we were directly responsible for its enforcement. But in view of the changed conditions I am not prepared to say that there will be any further relaxation, but I will say that we are bound to know that there has been a change in the conditions and that will no doubt be given some consideration.

I can very well see that if there were a combine among the lumbermen to prevent or restrict the manufacture of lumber or to unduly enhance the price, how you would be obliged to issue the order to have a larger amount manufactured, but when these conditions do not exist, as they do not exist at the present time, it would seem to me that it would involve a very great hardship upon the men who have paid, in many cases, large bonuses for these lands, who have carried them for some years, who have paid interest, which has amounted to a very large sum, rental and the cost of fireguards, to force these men to cut their timber when, by cutting that timber the increased amount thrown upon the market would reduce the price thereby entailing a very great loss. It would be a hardship that should not be inflicted on the lumber industry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might go as far as to say that if the conditions were changed so that the price of lumber had dropped very considerably before the 1st of December, I would feel very much inclined to give greater consideration with regard to the enforcement of the order.

While I know that the minister would have us understand that he has made a great effort to protect the country from fraud which might be perpetrated by means of obtaining timber limits, still, I can see that there are opportunities for fraud even in the present regulations. For instance, you send a cruiser to examine the limit and if he wishes to stand in with an intending purchaser he may report one value to the government and an entirely different and perhaps the true value to some friend who might be in collusion with him in order to obtain a valuable limit at a very low rate. The only way I see of further protecting the country would be to have a long period of advertising before the sale of the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite appreciate that but I think my hon. friend will find that there will be ample time between the date of advertising and the sale.
On section 54-conditions of license, protection of timber.

That is very important, to see that in taking off the timber the young timber is not destroyed and the timber is not cut too small. I think that cannot be too strongly enforced, particularly in view of the fact that there are a great many American lumbermen in the country now, and in their own country they have been very destructive. I think the department should take very great pains to see that the same destructive methods which have destroyed the timber limits on the other side of the line are not adopted here.
On section 59-permits to cut timber.

I wish to direct the minister's attention to the case of a man owning a small mill and getting a permit to cut on a square mile of timber. I know instances in which a mill cuts about double the quantity of timber daily that is consumed in the neighbourhood, and the mill owner would like the privilege of disposing of the surplus lumber to some of the lumber yards. I believe the regulations hold the mill owners down closely to the line, so that they are not allowed to sell to any but actual settlers. I would like an explanation from the minister on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This provision is in the regulations now, but we desire to embody it in the Act. We make it to meet a certain condition of affairs that prevails along the foot-hills of the Rockies, and in fact in all the partially wooded sections of the country. Where the prairie is near the edge of the wood, this provision becomes very valuable, because there may be settlers near timber but far from the mill, and to provide for the cutting of the timber by a portable mill is of great advantage to the settlers. So instead of putting this little berth up to competition or requiring any heavy bonus to be paid on it, we provide that the timber shall be cut on a permit granted without competition and at a fixed bonus for the year's work. But we do not think it fair or right that the man who gets that advantage should be allowed to compete with the mill owner who has had to pay for his limit in public competition, and may have had to pay a very large price. The permit is given as a matter of policy for the specific purpose of accommodating the settler, and therefore we do not consider that the mill owner has any grievance in not being in a position to deal with the lumber in the same way as the others. He has a special privilege, which was given to him for a special purpose, and he can always put himself in the position of the other limit hold-

ers by asking for the berth to be put up at public competition.

Suppose a settler has not the money to purchase the quantity of lumber he is allowed, and he wishes to turn over a portion of it to pay for the sawing of the other portion. I presume that is what the hon. member for Alberta had in mind when he spoke.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend must know that the settler is not entitled to pay for the cutting of his lumber by toll. He is entitled to get 9,000 odd feet of lumber for his own use; but he is not entitled to take 5,000 feet and allow the balance to go in payment for the cutting of that 5,000 feet.
Is there anything to prevent him doing that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, his affidavit requires him to state that the lumber is for his own use.
Does the affidavit stipulate that he must use the lumber on his premises in the construction of buildings ? Once he has the lumber, can he not dispose of it as he sees tit ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He again has been given a special privilege for a special purpose. That purpose is that he may get the lumber at cost for his own use, and he is of course subject to serious penalties if he traffics in the lumber.
On section 60-forfeiture and recovery of dues.

By subsection 2 the minister, before making an order for forfeiture, shall cause written notice to be given the licensee of his intention to do so, unless within thirty days after service the licensee show cause to the contrary. This time is too short. It ought to be at least ninety days. The licensee should have reasonable time before his license is forfeited. Many of them have invested very large sums and they ought to have time to turn around. In fact I would suggest six months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Ninety days would be fair, but the minister should give notice of the grounds of forfeiture.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I imagine that would be given as a matter of practice, but have no objection to inserting words to that effect.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Insert after the words ' so to do ' the words * upon the grounds set forth in such notice.'
Ninety days is rather short. If a man is delinquent in paying on real estate, he is subjected to no such drastic treatment as this.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
All he need do within the ninety days is file a petition to a judge.
364}

He has to show cause why his license should not be forfeited, and if he were given sufficient time he could fulfil the condition. Suppose the condition was to erect a mill and because of the financial stringency he found it impossible to do so. He gets notice that unless the mill is erected, his license will be forfeited. He could not erect a mill in ninety days.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The erection of a mill would not be any answer. Forfeiture has already taken place, and anything that occurs afterwards, would not save him, unless there is a clause enabling theThinister to discontinue proceedings.

Before making the order for forfeiture, the minister must give written notice of his intention, and the licensee has thirty days in which to show cause to the contrary. If he had the mill started, that would be cause to the contrary.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Suppose he made a fraudulent return, you should not let him remain six months and go on cutting the timber.
If he is guilty of fraud, you can take him at any time.

I know of many lumbermen notified by the Minister of the Interior to erect a mill, and it would be a hardship to ask them to do so at present, because there is no sale for their manufactured lumber. But the literal interpretation of that clause would leave it open to a minister to take arbitrary action, which would work hardship in the case of a man who had spent a large amount of money on the investment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Section 177 of chapter 55 of the revised statutes provides that a lease shall be liable to forfeiture and the minister may, without action, suit or other proceedings, and without compensation to the lessee, cancel the lease and make a new one. We are trying to get away from that very insensate provision. We want to make a provision that will be fair, equitable and workable, and I think the terms of this section will commend themselves to all parties except that there may be some question as to the time allowed. I think that ninety days is a fair and reasonable time to give the limit holder an opportunity to apply- and that is all this is for.
I recognize what the minister says as absolutely correct that it is more in the interest of the licensee than the former statute was.
But the original lease contained clauses something similar to this clause, which gave greater privileges to the licensee than was given by the original Act-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless in the case mentioned by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley), where there is a fraudulent return.
I think that when that is once proved, the leases should be absolutely forfeited.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But it must be proven and before that, there must be the accusation, reply and ail that. I think the ninety days is long enough in this case and that it is fair to all parties.
Why not give some discretion ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I have about all the discretion I want in this Bill.
On section 62-timber liable for dues.

I should think there ought to be even a penalty attached to that. If a man is trying to defraud the department, the dues he should be compelled to pay should be doubled-in New Brunswick, the man cutting on Crown lands is compelled to pay double dues.
On section 64-notes may be taken without affecting lien.
Does that mean that, after you have taken notes, you can seize the lumber in the hands of an innocent third party ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is wjiat it means.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A man might find part of his house liable for timber dues ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These sections are carried forward as they were in the old Act. I confess that they seem to be very drastic, but I did not dare to do much with them. I think they are there rather to scare people-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In terrorem.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes-rather than be enforced.	-
On section 67-if the timber has been mixed with other timber.
What is the meaning of the word ' dram ' in the sense in which you use it here ?

In making up timber on the Ottawa river, they have so many cribs to make a dram.
On section 70-disposal of seized timber.

I have not noticed any place where you provide that the parties seizing timber shall notify the owner or his agent. Timber might be seized and the owner know nothing about it until after the thirty days had expired.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The principle of the Act is to throw the burden entirely on the owner of the timber.
But it would not be fair to seize his timber and not let him know it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are many things in these regulations in regard to .timber that do not appeal to me as being fair. I have not altered these provisions. I suppose one reason of the provision is that in some cases it would be difficult to find the owner of the timber. The burden of keeping track of the timber rests upon the owner. The timber law takes it for granted that every timber man is a thief until he is proved innocent.

With the permission of the minister, I would like to refer again to section 52, as I was not here when the minister dealt with it. Has the lumberman any right to cut pulpwood? As a matter of fact, does the license contemplate the cutting of pulpwood?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It does not contemplate cutting anything that is smaller than the size mentioned.
So, in bidding for a timber limit, you do not know what the government is going to do.

Your license, when you get it, defines the sizes. But the government has the right to change those sizes.
Mr. PUG-SLEY. In advertising it, the description will say whether it is merchantable, and describe the size which the licensee would be allowed to cut.

The interpretation put on it by lumbermen is that when any pulpwood is cut on that limit it would be cut subject to the regulations made by the department, and the licensee would have the first rights. He has the best right to the timber subject to the regulations.
If subsequent regulations were made in regard to the cutting of pulpwood he would have the first right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In regard to section 52, I find that the officer in charge of the tim-

ber branch bas suggested some change in the wording. So we might say that section 52 shall stand for further consideration.
In connection with the description of the area within which we desire to have the pre-emption clause applied, the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. McCraney) suggested an adjustment of the eastern boundary. I would like to move a provision that would somewhat alter both the eastern and western boundaries, so that it would be before the committee for consideration when the Bill comes again. That relates to sections 27 and 28. The difference is that on the east side it is desired to use the third meridian. We leave the line of the third meridian going north. As it is proposed in this amendment, we continue on the third meridian instead of changing to the Saskatchewan river, and take the north line of township 44 throughout the whole district, from the third meridian to the Calgary and Edmonton Railway line, then take the Calgary and Edmonton Railway line for the western boundary until we reach the west line of range 26, and then follow the international boundary.
McCarthy. How much further south ? Does it go to the Calgary and Edmonton line?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Down the Calgary and
Edmonton line to Macleod and it then follows the range line due south to the boundary.
I would like to ask the minister if he intends including the area suggested by my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Jackson) and myself between Lake Winnipeg and Lake Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am just asking the committee to take into consideration the proposed amendment of the limits of this area. I was not suggesting the other, but when we take this up it will be open for consideration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment is as follows :
Commencing where the west line of range 26 west of the fourth principal meridian intersects the international boundary, thence east along the international boundary to its intersection with the Minneapolis, St. Paul and Sault Ste Marie Railway, thence north west along the said railway line to its junction with the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, thence west along the Canadian Pacific Railway to the third principal meridian, thence north along the third principal meridian to the north line of township U, thence west along the north line of township 44 to the Calgary & Edmonton Railway, thence south along' the Calgary & Edmonton Railway to its intersection with the west line of range 26 west of the fourth principal meridian, thence south along the west line of said range 26 to the international boundary.
Section allowed to stand.
Is that the only amendment that the minister intends to move to this section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the only amendment I desire to move but my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) and my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Jackson) spoke of another amendment which they will have an opportunity of moving, I presume, when we take this up in committee.
This section will stand?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I would ask the committee to revert to section 9 for the purpos^ of making, in subsection 3, the same provision with regard to including the width of road allowances in reference to the vicinity as we agreed to make in a section later on. I move that after the word ' miles ' in the seventh line of subsection 3 of section 9 to insert the words ' in a direct line exclusive of the width of the road allowances crossed in the measurement.'
Section as amended agreed to.
Progress reported.

stagedirection
speechtext: Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before the House adjourns, I would like to call your attention to the report of my remarks yesterday in connection with the Civil Service Bill. Speaking of the proposed increase in the salaries of the civil service, I am reported as follows :
The present Bill does not deal with that subject except in so far as it may be dealt with in the last section. I do not think it is one which should engage the attention of the government this session.
The last sentence is an entirely inaccurate statement of what I said. I expressly and distinctly stated that this subject should engage the attention of the government this session. May I ask what business will be taken up on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will continue the consideration of the Land Bill.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
